04_concepts/bellman-equation.title: Bellman equation
04_concepts/bellman-equation.content:
Bellman equation
The principle of optimality expressed as a fixed-point equation: the value of a state equals the immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state under optimal behavior.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram: foundational — underlies all cells
Failure mode addressed: none (this is the problem statement, not a solution method)
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
The Bellman equation decomposes the infinite-horizon optimization problem into a one-step recursion. Instead of optimizing over all future trajectories, you need only find a function V^* that is consistent with its own one-step lookahead. This is the control-theoretic principle of optimality expressed as an operator fixed point.
Formal definition
Bellman optimality equation (discrete-time stochastic):
V^*(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \left[ r(s, a, s') + \gamma V^*(s') \right]
Equivalently, in operator form: V^* = \mathcal{T} V^*, where \mathcal{T} is the Bellman optimality operator.
Bellman evaluation equation (for a fixed policy \pi):
V^\pi(s) = \sum_{a} \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \left[ r(s, a, s') + \gamma V^\pi(s') \right]
Connection to classical control
LQR solves the Bellman equation analytically for linear-quadratic problems: the value function is quadratic (V^*(x) = x^\top P x) and the Riccati equation is the Bellman equation in closed form. The HJB equation is the continuous-time analogue.
The Bellman operator \mathcal{T} is a \gamma-contraction in the sup-norm (Banach fixed-point theorem), guaranteeing that value iteration V_{k+1} = \mathcal{T} V_k converges geometrically to V^*.
Key limitation
Exact solution requires knowing the transition model P(s' \mid s, a) and reward r. When the model is unknown, we need sample-based approximations (TD learning, Q-learning). When the state space is large or continuous, we need function approximation in RL.
Related concepts
Dynamic programming | Value iteration | Policy iteration | TD learning | Q-learning | LQR | Curse of dimensionality
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1; Meyn (2022), Ch. 1
Classical control analogue: Anderson & Moore, Optimal Control, Ch. 2

04_concepts/deadly-triad.title: Deadly triad
04_concepts/deadly-triad.content:
Deadly triad
The combination of bootstrapping + off-policy learning + function approximation that provably causes divergence in value-based RL. No two of the three cause divergence; all three together do.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram: value-based × model-unknown (with function approximation)
Failure mode addressed: this is failure mode 1 (instability under function approximation)
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
Each ingredient alone is benign:

Bootstrapping (using value estimates in the target) speeds up learning
Off-policy data (learning from a different behavior policy) enables data reuse
Function approximation generalizes across states

But together, they interact to create positive feedback loops: the approximation error in the value estimate propagates through bootstrapped targets, and off-policy data means the training distribution doesn’t correct toward the true distribution. The result is divergence — value estimates blow up even on simple problems.
Formal statement
Baird’s counterexample (1995) provides a concrete 7-state MDP where semi-gradient TD(0) with linear function approximation diverges when all three ingredients are present. The key: the Bellman operator is no longer a contraction in the norm induced by the function approximation.
DQN as engineering response
DQN doesn’t eliminate the deadly triad — it engineers around it:





















DQN trickWhich part of triad it addressesExperience replay bufferDecorrelates consecutive samples; partially mitigates off-policy issuesTarget networkStabilizes the bootstrapped target by holding it fixed for N stepsDouble DQNReduces overestimation bias from bootstrapping + max operator
Key insight: these are stability tricks, not theoretical fixes. The deadly triad is still present. This is why deep RL training remains fragile.
Connection to classical control
The convergence of Value iteration rests on the Bellman operator being a contraction in \ell_\infty. Function approximation breaks this — the projected Bellman operator is no longer a contraction in general. This is a stability problem in the control-theoretic sense: a fixed-point iteration that diverges rather than converges.
Key limitation
No general solution exists. Current best practice combines the DQN stability tricks with careful hyperparameter tuning and monitoring for divergence.
Related concepts
Function approximation in RL | DQN | Failure modes of approximate RL | Q-learning | Bellman equation
References

Sutton & Barto (2018), Ch. 11 (“The deadly triad”)
Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1997) — convergence conditions for TD with FA
Baird (1995) — counterexample
Mnih et al. (2015) — DQN engineering response

04_concepts/failure-modes-of-approximate.title: Failure modes of approximate RL
04_concepts/failure-modes-of-approximate.content:
Failure modes of approximate RL
A teaching framework (not a complete taxonomy) organizing the dominant ways approximate RL breaks down. Introduced Week 7 as the central organizing artifact for the second half of the course.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram: cross-cutting — affects all cells with function approximation
Course first appearance: Week 7 (end of session)
Recurs: every theory session Weeks 8–15 opens with “which failure mode does today’s method address?”

The six failure modes
Three dominant (drive the value → policy → actor-critic narrative arc)





























#Failure modeAddressed byWeek formalized1Instability under function approximationDQN (replay, target network, double DQN)72High variance in policy optimizationBaselines, GAE, Actor-critic93Distribution shift in dataOffline RL, Residual RL12
Three secondary (real but not part of the main narrative arc)





























#Failure modeAddressed byWeek introduced4Insufficient explorationUCB, Thompson, curiosity4 (bandits)5Model bias in model-based methodsEnsemble models, MBPO116Reward misspecificationCBFs, CMDPs, reward shaping13
IMPORTANT: this is a teaching device, not ground truth
This framework privileges the three failure modes that drive the course narrative (value-based → policy-based → actor-critic). Other important failure modes exist that the course does not center:

Non-stationarity in deployment
Partial observability (touched in POMDP, not centered)
Multi-agent dynamics (out of scope)
Reproducibility and hyperparameter sensitivity (Week 15)

Always state this when presenting the framework. Students should leave knowing both the spine and its limits.
Shadow axes (planted before formalization)

Failure mode 3 (distribution shift) is planted in Week 7 (“replay works because distribution doesn’t shift much — if someone hands you logged data, this breaks”) and Week 9 (“on-policy by construction — the data-coverage problem from a different angle”)
Safety constraints (relevant to failure mode 6) are planted in Weeks 4, 7, 10 before Week 13 formalization

Related concepts
Deadly triad | DQN | Policy gradient theorem | Actor-critic | Offline RL | Safe RL | Model-based RL
References

No single reference: this framework is a course-specific synthesis
Instability: Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1997); Baird (1995)
Variance: Williams (1992); Schulman et al. (2016) GAE
Distribution shift: Levine et al. (2020) offline RL tutorial

index.title: RL in Robotics — Student Companion
index.content:
Reinforcement Learning in Robotics
240MAR45 · MSc in Automatic Control and Robotics · UPC Barcelona
This is the student companion site for the course: an interlinked knowledge base
of the core concepts, plus links to lecture notes, exercises, and practicals.


                  
                  How to use this site 
                  
                

Concepts are written to be self-contained and cross-linked. Start from
the unifying diagram below and follow the [[links]] by concept dependency,
not by lecture order. Use the search (top right) or the graph view to navigate.


The unifying diagram
Every method in this course lives in one cell of this table — what do we know
about the dynamics, and what are we trying to learn?

























Model knownModel unknownValue-basedDP / LQRQ-learning, DQNPolicy-basediLQRPolicy gradient (REINFORCE)HybridMPCActor-critic, Dyna
Start here

Bellman equation — optimality as a fixed-point recursion; the foundation
underlying every method in the course.
Deadly triad — why function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy
learning together can diverge.
Failure modes of approximate RL — the six failure modes that organize the
second half of the course.

Course framing
This course treats RL as approximate dynamic programming under uncertainty
about the dynamics. If you know LQR, Riccati, Bellman, and MPC, you already
have most of the scaffolding — RL fills in what to do when the model is unknown
or the state space is too large to solve exactly. RL is presented as one tool
among several, not a replacement for classical control.
